planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil; Silverhill is an old, cold-hardy satsuma selection long grown along the central Gulf Coast and is a good choice where winter lows occasionally dip lower than a typical satsuma can tolerate.

directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, siting it in a warm microclimate such as near a south-facing wall in the cooler parts of its range. This satsuma selection takes its name from the historic citrus-growing community of Silverhill in Baldwin County, Alabama, once a center of satsuma production shipped north by rail in the early 20th century. Like other satsumas, the small, deep-orange fruit is essentially seedless with loose, easy-to-peel skin and sweet, mild flesh, ripening from October into December. The tree is notably cold-hardy for a satsuma, tolerating brief dips into the low 20s°F once mature, which made it a mainstay of small Gulf Coast dooryard orchards.

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil; Okitsu ripens earlier than standard satsuma and its seedless, easy-peel fruit develops full sweetness ahead of most other citrus in the garden.

directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Selected at Japan's Okitsu horticultural research station as an early-ripening sport of common satsuma, this cultivar produces small, flattened, deep-orange fruit that colors and sweetens several weeks before standard satsuma, often ready by October. The seedless, loose-skinned segments are tender and richly sweet with low acidity, and the compact tree bears reliably from a young age. Its early ripening window makes it especially useful in areas where an early hard freeze can threaten later-maturing citrus.

common_name: Miho Satsuma (Early Compact Gulf South Satsuma)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil; Miho is an early-ripening satsuma widely planted in Gulf South home orchards for its compact size and reliably sweet, seedless fruit.

directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Another early-ripening Japanese satsuma selection similar in season to Okitsu, Miho has become one of the most commonly sold satsuma cultivars in Gulf Coast nurseries because of its naturally compact, rounded growth habit and dependable early crop of small, sweet, essentially seedless fruit. Fruit typically colors and ripens in October, ahead of standard-season satsumas, with loose rind that peels away easily in segments. The tree's smaller stature also makes it a good option for large containers that can be moved under cover during hard freezes.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after last frost in well-drained soil in full sun; Champagne is well adapted to hot, humid summers and performs reliably in Texas and Gulf South dooryard plantings.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Champagne is a light greenish-yellow fig long grown in Texas dooryards, prized for its thin skin, amber-pink pulp, and very sweet, honeyed flavor that many gardeners rank above darker-skinned figs for fresh eating. It fruits on both old and new wood, giving a small early-summer breba crop followed by a heavier main crop in late summer. Trees tolerate heat and humidity well and need little fertilizer once established, though a summer mulch layer helps even out soil moisture during fruit ripening. Protect young trees during hard freezes in the cooler end of its range; established plants regrow readily from the base after cold damage.
